courses.query: New York City Marathon elevation profile
courses.details: The NYC Marathon covers 26.2 miles through all five boroughs with 810 feet of elevation gain and 824 feet of loss, making it significantly more challenging than comparable marathons. The course features six major elevation segments: the Verrazzano-Narrows Bridge climb at the start (¾ mile at 4% gradient), relatively flat Brooklyn stretches, the demanding Pulaski and Queensboro bridges into Queens, a fast flat section on First Avenue, a grueling 2-mile climb up Fifth Avenue around mile 22, and rolling hills through Central Park to the finish near Tavern on the Green. Key race-day logistics include starting on Staten Island with early morning bridge crossings and crowd support, particularly energetic sections in Manhattan, and a quieter, mentally challenging final stretch through Central Park. The course's accumulation of bridges and hills in the final miles, combined with its undulating terrain throughout, makes it one of the slower World Marathon Majors, best approached for the iconic NYC experience rather than personal best times.

courses.query: Boston Marathon elevation gain loss profile
courses.details: The Boston Marathon is a point-to-point course dropping 1,239 feet overall while gaining 829 feet, resulting in a net descent of approximately 410 feet from Hopkinton (490 ft elevation) to Boston (10 ft elevation). The terrain is notably challenging despite the net downhill: it features a quad-punishing 300-foot plunge in the first 4 miles, rolling hills throughout the middle section, and the infamous Newton Hills with Heartbreak Hill (miles 16-21) presenting steep climbs of 80-100 feet that coincide with typical marathon fatigue. The final 5 miles offer recovery with a net descent into the city, but the course's combination of early downhill pounding and late-race climbs makes it one of the most difficult major marathons. Due to its point-to-point and net-downhill configuration, the Boston Marathon is ineligible for world record status, and performance is heavily influenced by wind and weather conditions.

courses.query: Philadelphia Marathon elevation profile steep uphills terrain
courses.details: The Philadelphia Marathon is a mostly flat course with 230 feet of total elevation gain and a maximum elevation of 136 ft, making it fast and Boston Qualifier-eligible. The most challenging section occurs between miles 8–13 through Fairmount Park, featuring a ~100-foot climb on Lansdowne Ave near the Zoo and rolling hills, though runners typically only lose 10–15 seconds on the uphill before gaining it back on the steep descent. The course includes additional climbs at the Manayunk turnaround (miles 18–21) and a final gradual uphill to the Museum of Art finish (miles 25.5–26.2), bookended by flat, fast sections on Benjamin Franklin Parkway and Kelly Drive. With the majority of elevation gain concentrated in the middle miles, runners can pace aggressively early and conserve energy for the final push to the iconic Art Museum steps.

courses.query: Philadelphia Marathon elevation profile and course difficulty
courses.details: The Philadelphia Marathon is a mostly flat road course with a maximum elevation of 136 feet and minimum of 7 feet, featuring only two major hills in the 8th and 10th miles. The course includes rolling hills throughout, particularly notable between miles 15-20 near the turnaround point and in the Manayunk section (miles 19-21), which also provides excellent crowd support. Despite the elevation profile suggesting an uphill finish, runners typically experience a slight downhill feel crossing the finish line. With a course score of 98.46, Philadelphia ranks among Pennsylvania's fastest marathons, making it ideal for personal records when combined with favorable race-day temperature and humidity conditions.

courses.query: elevation profile and hilliness of New York City half marathon course
courses.details: The United Airlines NYC Half Marathon is a 13.1-mile course starting in Brooklyn's Prospect Park with two early hills, including the challenging Battle Pass Hill (6.8% max grade). The route crosses the Brooklyn Bridge into Manhattan, then runs roughly 4 flat miles along the FDR Drive before climbing gradually through Midtown and Times Square. The final miles feature rolling terrain through Central Park to the finish near Tavern on the Green. Overall elevation gain is approximately 125 feet, with an estimated pace slowdown of 1.8% compared to a flat course, making it a fast and manageable half marathon despite the rolling terrain.

The Philadelphia Marathon is generally considered a relatively flat course with net zero elevation gain, ranging from 7 feet to 136 feet elevation with start/finish at 33 feet. The only significant climbing occurs between miles 8-10, with the biggest climb just after the Zoo on Lansdowne Avenue, followed by a major downhill onto MLK Drive around mile 11. Runners may encounter some smaller rolling hills throughout the course, particularly between miles 18-21, and a gentle incline in the final mile. While elevation maps can make the course appear hillier than it actually is due to 50-foot increments, some GPS watches register between 600-650 feet of total climbing depending on routing variations.
